newsitem.title: UK: UK inflation falls...but for how much longer?.
newsitem.headline: UK inflation falls...but for how much longer?.

text.p: A fall in British retail price inflation in March was welcomed by the financial markets on Thursday but with consumers still spending freely price pressures could pick up soon, analysts said.
Official figures showed headline RPI edged down to 2.6 percent in the year to March, from 2.7 in February. Underlying inflation crept back to 2.7 percent year-on-year, from 2.9.
But economists said hefty increases in household goods and clothing and footwear prices suggested high street retailers were starting to take healthy consumer spending for granted.
"Inflation will nudge down a little further before bottoming out but the 2.5 percent target will be very difficult to hold," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
Underlying inflation, at 2.7 percent, was at its lowest level since May 1995, but that simply demonstrates the difficulty the government has had in achieving its 2.5 percent target.
Gardiner said the 2.5 percent leap in household goods prices in March, coupled with a 2.0 percent rise in clothing and footwear prices, was a surprise.
"I thought the very soft input prices would hold off margin building for a while," he said. Producer output prices rose only 1.0 percent in the year to March.
Gardiner said the idea that retailers profit margins had been exceptionally weak in recent years was something of a myth.
"But these figures suggest some retailers are taking the opportunity to push margins. This reinforces my suspicion that the myth of weakness in profit margins is being buried."
James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said high street prices were undergoing a natural rebound from Christmas and January sales to some extent.

He said rising clothing, shoes and household goods prices contradicted evidence from the British Retail Consortium that retauk sales growth moderated in the year to March. But he agreed the numbers were strong.
"And what was even more disappointing was the drop in inflation was largely driven by lower food prices. That's basically down to the strong pound," Barty said.
The pound has rocketed by about 17 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August, cutting import prices in the process.

Thursday's figures from the Office for National Statistics showed food prices dropped 0.6 percent in March with seasonal food prices down 2.6 percent, the biggest drop for the month of March since 1957.
With rain a scarce commodity in Britain right now -- the country is suffering its worst drought in more than 200 years -- domestic crops may be hit in the summer, pushing prices back up.
"Of course it's a bit early to say, but food prices could be a bit rocky by the summer," Barty said.

Nonetheless, Barty said underlying inflation, excluding mortgage payments, would drop to 2.5 percent later this year as sterling continues to depress import prices. "The problems come next year when the effect of the pound wears off," he said.
He said whoever is in the Treasury after May 1 elections should put up interest rates soon.

But Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown would face the same problem as Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke -- "an unbelievably strong currency. He will move carefully, in quarters rather than half-points," Barty said.
Both men have backed themselves into a corner by ruling out direct tax increases so monetary policy is the only policy lever to restrain a bubbling domestic economy.

Stewart Robinson, economist at Lombard Street Research, said the strength of consumer demand would allow retailers to push up prices, no matter what input costs do. He said a half-point increase in six percent base rates was required straight after the election.
"I think we'll see inflation trough in the next two or three months. After that, it will be on quite a firmly rising trend," he told Reuters Financial Television.
